findings.claim: Backup code comparison uses indexOf, which is case-sensitive, and only '-' is stripped from the input. Valid codes typed in a different case or with whitespace are rejected, for example uppercase from iOS auto-capitalize. The same comparison appears in disable.ts and BackupCode.tsx.

verifier.reason: Codes are stored as lowercase hex (apps/web/pages/api/auth/two-factor/totp/setup.ts:61) and matched with exact `backupCodes.indexOf(input.replaceAll("-", ""))` at packages/features/auth/lib/next-auth-options.ts:144 and apps/web/pages/api/auth/two-factor/totp/disable.ts:61, with no trim or lowercase anywhere, so uppercase or whitespace-padded input is rejected. BackupCode.tsx holds no comparison, only the un-normalised input field (no autoCapitalize off), so that part of the claim is loosely worded.

findings.claim: Backup code consumption is a non-atomic read, decrypt, check, null-slot and write-back, with no transaction, lock or compare-and-swap. Concurrent requests can both accept the same backup code, and last-write-wins can restore a code that was already consumed.

verifier.reason: packages/features/auth/lib/next-auth-options.ts:73-102 reads the user with a plain findUnique, then lines 139-156 decrypt, indexOf, null the slot and write the whole blob back with an unconditional prisma.user.update keyed only on id; there is no transaction, lock or conditional where on the old value. Two concurrent logins can therefore both accept the same code, and two logins using different codes can overwrite each other so a consumed code is restored.

findings.claim: Backup codes are stored as reversible ciphertext via symmetricEncrypt instead of one-way hashes, so they can be recovered if the DB and the app key are exposed.

verifier.reason: Backup codes are stored as AES-256 ciphertext of the JSON array via symmetricEncrypt (apps/web/pages/api/auth/two-factor/totp/setup.ts:68, packages/features/auth/lib/next-auth-options.ts:154) and recovered in plaintext with symmetricDecrypt for comparison (next-auth-options.ts:139-144, apps/web/pages/api/auth/two-factor/totp/disable.ts:58), so anyone holding the DB and CALENDSO_ENCRYPTION_KEY can read them. This matches how the existing twoFactorSecret is already stored under the same key, so it adds little exposure beyond what that threat model already allows.

findings.claim: The component exported from BackupCode.tsx is named `TwoFactor` instead of `BackupCode`. It collides with the existing TwoFactor component in DevTools, stack traces and imports.

verifier.reason: apps/web/components/auth/BackupCode.tsx:7 declares `export default function TwoFactor`, the same name as apps/web/components/auth/TwoFactor.tsx:8, so both show as `TwoFactor` in DevTools and stack traces. Imports are unaffected, since it is a default export that callers import as `BackupCode`.

findings.claim: The object URL created for the backup-codes download is only revoked when a new one is generated. It is never revoked when the modal is closed, reset or unmounted, so the blob leaks.

verifier.reason: The only `URL.revokeObjectURL` call is at apps/web/components/settings/EnableTwoFactorModal.tsx:98, just before a new URL is created at :99; `resetState` (:71-75) clears neither `backupCodesUrl` nor `backupCodes`, and the sole `useEffect` (:157-161) has no cleanup, so the blob holding the plaintext backup codes lives until the document unloads.

findings.claim: `req.body.backupCode.replaceAll()` is called on an unvalidated body. A truthy non-string backupCode throws a TypeError and returns 500 instead of 400.

verifier.reason: apps/web/pages/api/auth/two-factor/totp/disable.ts:48 only checks that `req.body.backupCode` is truthy, and line 61 then calls `.replaceAll("-", "")` on it with no type check, schema validation or try/catch in the handler. A JSON body such as `{"backupCode": 123}` therefore throws an uncaught TypeError (a 500) instead of the 400 IncorrectBackupCode, though only for an authenticated user with 2FA enabled, stored backup codes and a correct password.

findings.claim: `JSON.parse(symmetricDecrypt(...))` on backupCodes is unguarded. Corrupted data can throw or return a non-array, which crashes the authorize/disable flow with a 500.

verifier.reason: apps/web/pages/api/auth/two-factor/totp/disable.ts:58 and packages/features/auth/lib/next-auth-options.ts:139-141 call JSON.parse(symmetricDecrypt(user.backupCodes, ...)) with no try/catch or array check, so corrupted or re-keyed data throws uncaught (a 500 in disable.ts; in authorize next-auth surfaces it as a login error rather than a literal 500). It needs server-written data to be corrupted or the encryption key changed, and the adjacent code at disable.ts:51 and :77 already throws InternalServerError for comparable bad states.

findings.claim: Migration timestamp 20230804153419 is older than existing migrations such as 20230828094603, which causes Prisma migration-order drift.

verifier.reason: The patch adds packages/prisma/migrations/20230804153419_add_backup_codes/migration.sql (change.patch:679-686), while the untouched packages/prisma/migrations/20230828094603_add_include_calendar_event/migration.sql already exists, so databases already at 20230828 apply it out of timestamp order.
